p.b:
This kite of paper took to flight,

a boy stood holding fast the string.

The wind lifted it up on high,

the sky called out to it to fly.

When it rose his heart would race,

when it fell his breath would catch.

Someone's string cut across the air,

and it was lost, drifting there.

The boy ran after where it went,

and found it fallen on a roof.

It was a little torn, but still,

he mended it with care and will.

Tomorrow this same kite will rise,

the string made stronger than before.

For falling too can teach a thing -

that lesson now the boy knew well.

p.d: गद्यांश: The Train That Came Once a Day
p.b:
The railway line passed just outside the village, but the station was in the town, fifteen kilometres away. So when the whole family finally set out to visit Uncle's house by train, everyone had to wake at four in the morning. The luggage was loaded onto a bullock cart and they left while it was still dark.

At the station the first thing they saw was the queue for tickets. Father bought the tickets and Mother gathered all the luggage in one place. People were hurrying in every direction on the platform. Some carried bundles on their heads, some carried children on their shoulders. The tea seller's voice rang out again and again - 'Chai garam, chai garam!'

When the train arrived it looked enormously long. Getting into the compartment was not easy, because of the crowd. Somehow they all got inside and found seats. Getting a seat by the window was a great thing, because fields, rivers and small stations would be visible all the way.

When the train moved there was first a jerk, and then the speed grew slowly. The fields slipped behind and the birds sitting on the wires flew away. By the time they reached Uncle's town it was evening. The day was very tiring, but the world seen through the train window felt completely new.

Before the station wakes, the engine breathes,

a long grey sigh along the empty platform,

and somewhere in the yard a shunter calls

to nobody in particular at all.

The carriages are cold. The windows hold

a thin blue film of night that will not go,

and in each frame a different dark is kept -

a field, a wall, a tree, a piece of sky.

Then something changes. Not a whistle yet,

but a small tightening along the floor,

a settling of iron against iron,

as though the whole long train had drawn a breath.

The town begins to slide away behind,

the water tower leans and passes on,

and light arrives in pieces through the trees -

one branch, one fence, one road, one field of wheat.

By noon we will be strangers to this hour,

asleep against the window with our coats,

forgetting how the morning came apart

and put itself together, mile by mile.

p.d: गद्यांश: The Mango Tree in the School Yard
p.b:
There was a mango tree in the corner of the school yard, so old that no one could remember who had planted it. Its trunk was wide enough for three children to hold hands around, and its branches spread over a large part of the ground. In summer the shade under it was the coolest place in the whole school.

Every year the tree gave fruit, but the mangoes hung high up where no child could reach them. The headmaster had a long bamboo pole with a small net tied to the end. When the fruit was ready, he called the whole school together and plucked the mangoes one by one while everyone counted aloud.

The mangoes were then shared equally among all the children, whatever their class or their marks. Nobody was given more because he was clever, and nobody was given less because he was slow. The children who lived far away were given their share early so that the fruit would not spoil on the long walk home.

One year a storm came in the night and broke one of the largest branches. The next morning the children stood around the tree in silence. The headmaster did not have the broken branch carried away. Instead he had it cut into small pieces and gave one piece to each child to take home.

Years later, when those children had grown up, many of them planted a mango tree in their own yard. They could not always say why. But when asked, most of them spoke of a school yard, a shade in summer, and a fruit that was shared equally.

Meera had grown up believing that her father's work was the most important job on the coast. Every evening, when the sun sank behind the headland, he climbed the one hundred and twelve steps of the lighthouse tower, trimmed the wick, and set the great lamp turning. A single beam swept across the dark water, and ships a long way out adjusted their course towards safety.

It was not an easy life. In the monsoon the wind tore at the shutters and the sea threw spray as high as the gallery rail. Twice the supply boat failed to come for a whole month, and the family lived on rice, dried fish and whatever grew in the small garden behind the keeper's cottage. Meera learned to repair the lamp mechanism when she was fourteen, because her father's hands had begun to shake and he could no longer hold the fine tools steady.

When the government decided to automate the light, an engineer arrived with crates of instruments and stayed for three weeks. He was polite, and he explained everything carefully, but Meera noticed that he never once climbed to the lamp room at night. The new system was reliable, he said. It would never need trimming.

The night the light was switched over, Meera stood on the gallery and watched the automatic beam turn. It was steadier than her father's had ever been. There was no flicker, no moment when the flame guttered in a sudden draught. It was, she admitted to herself, better.

Two winters later a fishing boat came ashore in a storm. Its engine had failed and the crew had been guided in by the beam. The captain climbed up to thank them, and when he saw Meera's father sitting in the doorway with his hands wrapped around a cup of tea, he asked him how long he had kept the light. Forty years, her father said. The captain looked at the automatic lamp and then back at the old man, and said that he had never once thought about who was up there. He had only ever trusted that someone was.

p.d: गद्यांश: The Night Bus to the City
p.b:
The night bus to the city left our town at ten o'clock. It was the only bus that ran after dark, and it carried the same handful of people every night: two nurses who worked the early shift at the city hospital, a man who sold vegetables at the morning market, and a few students like me who had come home for the holidays.

The first time I travelled on it, I was nervous. My aunt had warned me that the night bus was full of strangers. But by the second journey I knew the conductor by name, and by the fifth I had a seat of my own - the one behind the driver, where the window opened properly.

The road out of town was dark, and the bus lit it up in short pieces. Every few kilometres we passed a village where a single bulb hung outside a tea stall, and someone was always there, waiting. Sometimes they got on; sometimes they only waved.

What I remember most, though, is not the road but the talk. The nurses taught us which hospitals paid on time. The vegetable seller told us the price of onions in four different markets. And somewhere around midnight, when the bus grew quiet, someone would begin to sing, and the rest of us would join in badly.

I have travelled on faster buses since then, and on trains with clean sheets. But I have never again been part of a journey where everyone knew everyone else's business, and where nobody minded.

p.d: गद्यांश: The Post Office: An Old Friend
p.b:
There was a time when a letter was the only way to reach a loved one living far away. The post office was the most important place in the village. Every morning the postman set out with a bundle of letters and walked from house to house. People waited for him, hoping that a letter had arrived for their family.

Writing a letter was an art. Choosing the paper, dipping the pen in ink, writing neatly, folding it into an envelope and sticking the stamp - every step demanded care. A reply could take weeks to arrive, so every word was chosen thoughtfully. When a letter came, the whole family gathered around it and read it again and again.

Today mobile phones and the internet have almost erased that distance. A message arrives in a moment and a reply comes back just as fast. Many post offices no longer see crowds of letters.

And yet the post office is not useless. Government documents, examination forms, bank accounts and the small savings of villages are still handled by it. Where the internet has not reached, the post office remains the only trusted link. The technology has changed, but the responsibility of reaching people remains the same.

The clouds arrive like letters,

folded grey and heavy,

and the sky opens them slowly

over the roof of our house.

The first drop writes a word

on the dusty window pane,

the second one a sentence,

and soon the page is rain.

The paper boats we folded

are sailing down the lane,

each one carrying a message

that will never be the same.

My mother hangs the wet clothes

in a line beneath the shade,

and reads the sky each morning

like a letter to be weighed.

When the clouds have said their business,

they fold themselves and go,

leaving the world rewritten

in a hand we barely know.

In those winter evenings,

we sat inside the quilt,

and listened to the stories

that grandmother told.

There were kings and there were queens,

there were thieves and watchmen too,

and a tree inside the forest

whose roots went very deep.

Grandmother's voice was quiet,

but the story ran quite fast,

and whenever she fell silent

we all shouted out for more.

Now grandmother is far away,

and those evenings come no more,

but the stories that she told me

are still living here inside.

The banyan standing at the crossroads,

a witness of a hundred years.

Its roots went deep into the ground,

its branches climbed where clouds are found.

In summer heat it offered shade,

and weary travellers were laid.

The birds have built their nests in it,

the children made their rest in it.

When rain came down it held the water,

when storms came hard it stood still firmer.

Cut it down and it stays mute -

yet the village breathes through this old root.

Now the road must widen here,

a new building must appear.

But ask this question, friend, once more -

where will you find that shade before?
